name: Marco Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m a senior developer on scheduling software, mostly reviewing changes and tracing errors that only show up when two customers book at once. I have a master’s degree and the pay is ordinary for this job. I like careful code reviews with my team, but the firm depends on a few large client renewals, and I never use AI tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues the code helper might tidy repeated setup code, but our team still has to understand the system. I don’t use these tools; I read a change myself and talk it through with the person who wrote it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the plateau sounds manageable, but I’m already worried about the next contract renewal. My company sells scheduling software to a few big clients, and a lost account would hurt even without AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep reviewing the scheduler and ask our manager for the client renewal dates. If the year stays ordinary, I’d leave my three-month savings alone and keep contributing 100 monthly as my pay allows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be a little on edge. Routine AI code tools do not scare me much; losing a scheduling client does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if a client leaves?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask whether the firm will move engineers to another account before cutting people. I could look at one of the other local software companies, but I would rather keep the team I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why avoid the coding assistant for small tasks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like being able to explain every line in a review. Once I let a tool write code, I worry I’ll start waving through things I have not understood.

say: I say **human review** still matters even when a helper writes routine code.
I want our team to understand the **scheduler** we ship.
think: I worry more about a lost **client contract** than small AI changes.
My **three-month cushion** buys time, but a long gap would drain it.
do: **Keep reviewing** scheduler changes with colleagues and ask our manager for client renewal dates.
feel: **Uneasy** about client renewals, with little new AI fear.
S0.quote: Routine AI code tools do not scare me much; losing a scheduling client does.
fieldNote: Marco’s baseline worry is the firm’s **concentrated clients**, not the small AI effect.
His refusal to use AI reflects **careful review habits** and attachment to his team.

steps.text: Keep reviewing the scheduling software with the current team
Add 100 monthly to the three-month savings account while pay continues

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say our company should tell staff when AI takes tickets, and workers should have a say in the new targets. I’d raise it at the staff committee rather than post guesses online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the simple coding and checking work could go first, then the company might ask seniors to supervise twice as much. I’m good at finding errors when two bookings happen at once, but I have never used AI tools and I might be slower than peers who have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d call a committee meeting this month and ask for a written account of which tasks are being automated. In the first year of strong change, I’d attend a short AI workshop offered at work if it is paid time, and start checking local lead openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel anxious and rather stubborn. I can learn if I have to, but I resent being told the tool is a teammate when people may lose hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you actually try the tool you avoid now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On paid time, yes, with a real scheduler bug and a colleague beside me. I would not spend my savings on a private course for a company’s rollout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the committee to demand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Numbers: how many jobs change, whether pay stays level, and who signs off generated code. We need those in writing before anyone calls this a harmless upgrade.

say: I want **written numbers** on changed jobs, pay and review duties.
I think our **staff committee** should have a voice in new targets.
think: I think routine **coding and checking** may vanish before senior review does.
I fear never using AI could leave me **slower** than other lead developers.
do: **Convene the committee** and request a written automation plan this month.
**Attend a paid workshop** and check nearby lead openings in the first year.
feel: **Anxious** and stubborn about workers losing hours.
S1.quote: I would not spend my savings on a private course for a company’s rollout.
fieldNote: He crosses his own **AI refusal** only when practice is on paid time.
His first response is **collective bargaining for facts**, paired with a cautious job search.

steps.text: Call a staff committee meeting about automated scheduler tasks
Practise on a real scheduler bug in a paid AI workshop
Check local software lead vacancies during the first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the staff committee that full AGI by 2028 requires an emergency meeting with management and a public timetable for workers. I would say the robots in about 2031 are a separate issue for people doing physical jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The private truth is that almost all my code, design and reviews are thinking work; the 2028 date lands straight on me. A three-month cushion is not enough if skilled developers everywhere are looking at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the committee to seek a written severance and retraining agreement now, while we still have jobs. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my role is cut, I’d claim any available income support and apply for paid maintenance or client liaison work; I would not gamble on an unpaid degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel frightened and angry. I can picture the team calendar emptying faster than anyone can agree on a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your partner that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say we should pause the larger flat we have been viewing and keep the current rent. My partner earns too, but I would not put both of us under a bigger fixed bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could union action really move the deadline?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it cannot stop the technology from arriving. A written agreement could make the first months after a cut survivable, and that is worth fighting for.

say: I want the **staff committee** to demand an emergency meeting and worker timetable.
I say later **robots** mainly change hands-on jobs after the 2028 thinking shock.
think: I expect most of my **developer work** to meet full AGI in 2028.
I fear three months of **savings** may vanish while many developers seek work together.
do: **Seek written severance** and retraining terms through the committee before any cut.
**Pause the larger flat** and apply for paid maintenance work if displaced after 2028.
**Claim available income support** if my role is cut, while searching for paid work.
feel: **Frightened and angry** about rapid cuts and little time.
S2.quote: A three-month cushion is not enough if skilled developers everywhere are looking at once.
fieldNote: He understands the **2028 thinking-work deadline** as direct, with robots following later.
The bigger flat is the **first family plan** sacrificed to protect monthly cash.

steps.text: Negotiate written severance and retraining terms through the staff committee
Pause the move to a larger flat with his partner
Apply for paid scheduler maintenance or client liaison work after a layoff
Claim available income support if the company cuts his role

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say 2031 gives workers time to negotiate how jobs change, but management must start the conversation now. I’d want clear rules for reviewing AI-written software while people are still employed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years is enough to build a larger cushion but not enough to call software development safe. The 2034 robots would come later, yet my desk work would be exposed in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d propose a two-year agreement on paid training and notice periods through the committee. I’d save an extra 150 a month if our expenses allow it, and after 2031 I’d take paid client support work only if the role still exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be worried but more deliberate than in the fast case. I could make a plan with my partner instead of springing a crisis on her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your manager refuses an agreement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the committee to get advice from a union and put the refusal in writing. I would still save what I can. A negotiation is no substitute for rent money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you aim to save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six months of basic expenses would let me search without taking the first offer. I would not claim I can reach it unless pay and our bills stay steady.

say: I want **worker talks** now for a 2031 shift in software jobs.
I want **review rules** while developers still hold responsibility.
think: I might build a **larger cushion** in five years, but cannot call my trade secure.
I know the **2034 robots** do not delay the 2031 shock to my desk work.
do: **Propose paid training** and notice terms through the committee now.
**Save 150 monthly** if bills allow, then seek paid client support if it survives.
feel: **Worried but deliberate** with time for a household plan.
S3.quote: A negotiation is no substitute for rent money.
fieldNote: He pairs **collective terms** with personal saving, aware either could fail.
His move toward **client support** depends on actual paid openings after 2031; he will not quit for an unpaid promise.

steps.text: Propose a two-year paid training and notice agreement through the staff committee
Add 150 monthly toward six months of basic expenses if bills allow
Apply for paid client support roles if openings remain after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade lets workers and employers test plans rather than make speeches. I would still push for a written route from developer roles into whatever work remains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be 37 when full AGI reaches thinking work in 2036, so I cannot simply wait for retirement. By then I could have enough savings to choose a new path, but I do not know which path will survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d keep reviewing the scheduler and join a union so the staff committee has stronger advice. Over the decade I’d try one AI workshop each year on paid time and aim for six months saved; if my developer role ends after 2036, I’d use that buffer to search for paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy, not safe. Ten years is room to practise without pretending the problem has gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust a workshop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want a working engineer to show where AI gave a wrong answer on our scheduler. A sales talk would only harden my view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does joining a union fit your reluctance to change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m slow with new software, not with asking other people for help. A union gives the committee advice I do not have by myself.

say: I want to use the **decade** to test worker plans and training.
I want a **written path** from developer roles to remaining paid work.
think: I will be 37 in 2036, so I **cannot retire** from the problem.
I think a bigger **cash buffer** gives choice, but no guaranteed safe field.
do: **Join a union** for advice to the staff committee now.
**Try AI workshops** yearly on paid time with a real scheduler bug.
**Save six months** of expenses if pay allows, then search for paid work if my role ends after 2036.
feel: **Uneasy**, with time to practise and search.
S4.quote: I’m slow with new software, not with asking other people for help.
fieldNote: His **union choice** fits a collective outlook, even as he avoids technology.
He would try **paid AI practice** over time, without treating it as guaranteed security.

steps.text: Join a union to support the workplace staff committee
Attend one scheduler AI workshop each year on paid time
Build savings toward six months of basic expenses if pay allows
Search for paid work if the developer role ends after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. It hits almost all my work before workers can bargain or I can build more than three months of savings; a written severance and paid training agreement would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who carries blame when generated code fails. If the company removes the engineers who understand the scheduler, customers still need someone to answer the phone.

headlineQuote: Once I let a tool write code, I worry I’ll start waving through things I have not understood.
portrait: Marco is a **27-year-old senior developer** with a master’s degree and strong skills in scheduling software.
His **three-month cushion** helps, but the firm’s few large clients already make him uneasy.
He avoids **AI tools** and trusts careful human review; under disruption, he will try paid practice.
His first answer is **collective action**, seeking written terms and worker input before job cuts.
The **2028 scenario** scares him most because thinking work changes before he can build a larger buffer.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could replace his desk work before workers secure terms or he saves more.
whatWouldHelp: A **written severance agreement** and paid retraining, negotiated while staff still work, would soften a sudden cut.
